title: Patenting Quantum Computing Innovations – Part 3: Implementing a Logical Qubit in a Surface Code - Quantum Computing Report
gist: A short legal worked example (written by Covington & Burling special counsel Sinan Utku, though the record's author field says Doug Finke) arguing that a generic surface-code logical-qubit claim risks being ruled an ineligible 'abstract idea' under the US Mayo/Alice test, because error correction with redundant bits long predates quantum computing. The defense is to draft claims as improvements to a specific quantum computing system, tied to particular hardware, and not to 'a logical qubit' as such. For investors, a QEC patent's value depends heavily on how it is claimed.

insights.claim: Surface codes are a leading class of quantum error correction codes likely to be used in fault-tolerant quantum computing: many physical data qubits jointly encode one logical qubit in a nonlocal, topologically protected way.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Surface-code QEC is the expected route to fault tolerance, so IP around it is central to how quantum hardware firms can defend their position.
insights.quote: Surface codes are a promising class of quantum error correction codes that will likely be used in fault-tolerant quantum computing.

insights.claim: A surface-code logical qubit is built and maintained in five steps: configure data qubits on a 2D lattice, interleave ancilla qubits that measure stabilizers of neighboring data qubits, periodically run stabilizer measurements, derive error syndromes, and apply corrective operations. Classical decoding algorithms infer where the errors are.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: This generic claim template is what competitors' patents may resemble. Claims this broad are the weakest when challenged, as the rest of the article shows.

insights.claim: A generic surface-code logical-qubit patent could be challenged under US patent law as directed to the abstract idea of 'error correction using redundant bits', a concept used for a long time in classical communication and computing.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Broad quantum error correction patents held by quantum companies may be more fragile in litigation than their headline scope suggests. Discount IP moats built on generic QEC claims.
insights.quote: the invention might be found to be directed to the abstract idea of error correction using redundant bits

insights.claim: Going only by its generic specification, a surface-code logical-qubit invention probably has no good argument under step 2 of the Mayo/Alice framework, meaning no inventive element that would turn the abstract idea into eligible subject matter, because it rests on error-correction concepts from classical computing.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The 'inventive concept' fallback is weak for QEC patents, so their eligibility depends on the 'technological improvement' argument and on claims tied to specific hardware.

insights.claim: A quantum error correction patent is more likely to be ruled an abstract idea if it is not tied to a specific quantum hardware platform or set of components. Including hardware elements generally raises the odds of patent eligibility.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: In quantum IP due diligence, check whether QEC claims name specific hardware (qubit modality, components). Hardware-tied claims are more defensible, but they are narrower and apply only to one platform.
insights.quote: generally, inclusion of hardware elements increases the likelihood that the invention will be found to be patent eligible

insights.claim: Tying a claim to hardware does not guarantee eligibility: in the Symantec case, an invention containing only mechanical (hardware) elements was still found patent ineligible.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Even hardware-heavy quantum patents carry some eligibility risk in litigation, so do not treat any QEC patent portfolio as a certain moat.
insights.quote: the invention in Symantec included only mechanical, i.e., hardware, elements and was nevertheless found to be patent ineligible

insights.claim: A patentee can defend a surface-code patent against an abstractness challenge by arguing that the surface code and the resulting logical qubit improve the functioning of the claimed quantum computing system. The USPTO's MPEP § 2106.04(d)(1) (Nov. 2024) treats improving 'the functioning of a computer' or another technical field as a patent-eligible practical application.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The strongest quantum QEC patents are written as improvements to a system or device. Look for this framing when judging how durable a company's error-correction IP is.

insights.claim: A patent claim directed just to 'a logical qubit', and not to a quantum computing system, is harder to defend. A logical qubit is not a device that can itself be improved and is arguably an abstraction, so the 'improves the machine' argument does not easily apply.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The claim scope a company announces (for example, 'we patented our logical qubit') can be legally weaker than it sounds. Claims on system-level embodiments with particular details are more robust.
insights.quote: A logical qubit is not a device that itself is capable of improvement and is arguably itself an abstraction.

insights.claim: Adding specific details that narrow a quantum error correction invention should improve its chances of being found patent eligible. This trades breadth of coverage for survivability under Alice.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Quantum IP moats face a breadth-versus-validity tradeoff: broad foundational QEC claims are the most exposed, while narrow hardware-specific claims survive but block fewer competitors.
insights.quote: specifying details that particularize the invention should increase the odds of a finding of patent eligibility
